title: POC: Benchmark harness integration + streaming vs batched behavior
summary: Scoping call to define POC benchmark plan and harness integration. Customer wants both streaming and non-streaming benchmarks, success criteria tied to p95 latency and cost per 1k tokens; workload sizing based on production traces, and an agreed ramp plan with concrete scripts to run in their environment and in Redwood's test cluster.
topics: load harness choices and sample scripts
benchmark metrics and success criteria (p50/p95/p99, cost)
next_steps: Redwood to send example harness (k6 + Python async) and small dataset by 2025-04-13
Quantara to provide 2 weeks of anonymized request traces and sample prompts by 2025-04-17
Schedule 1-hour baseline run with non-streaming at 200 qps on 2025-04-24
Follow-up call to review baseline / streaming delta on 2025-04-28
action_items: Daniel Park - share 'benchmark-harness.zip' with k6 scenarios and async python clients - due 2025-04-13
Alex Chen - export 14-day production trace (anonymized) and sample prompt sets - due 2025-04-17
Maya Collins - propose pilot pricing/rate limits and secure sandbox creds - due 2025-04-14
Priya Rao - confirm network egress constraints and VPC peering windows - due 2025-04-16
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-10 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~58m | Attendees: Maya Collins (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood Solutions), Alex Chen (Quantara ML Eng), Priya Rao (Quantara SRE), Michael Thompson (Quantara CTO)

[00:00] Maya Collins: All right, thanks everyone for joining. Quick note: recording is on. We wanted to focus today on benchmark planning and how you want to wire your scripts into our harness and also validate streaming vs non-streaming behavior, is that right Alex?

[00:18] Alex Chen: Yeah that's correct. The main goal for Quantara is to understand tail latency and cost at our peak mix. We have a mix of short prompts (30-80 tokens) and longer analysis prompts (~800-1,200 tokens) and then a lot of streaming style UIs where tokens stream while the user sees partial results.

[00:36] Daniel Park: Cool. To frame this, we usually treat three benchmark vectors: 1) short interactive QPS (low tokens), 2) long generation throughput (high tokens per request), and 3) streaming interactions where we care about first-byte latency and incremental token latency. For POC scoping we need your trace so we can size concurrency, average token lengths, and the percentiles.

[00:55] Priya Rao: We can provide anonymized traces. One thing: our infra team is concerned about the test harness hitting production databases by accident; we'll scrub user ids but also want guidance on safe data handling.

[01:10] Sofia Ruiz: Good flag. For the harness we recommend synthetic prompt substitution where you keep prompt shape and length but replace PII. We'll include a small script to do that. Also we'll provide a sample dataset you can run locally.

[01:28] Michael Thompson: Our success criteria are pretty practical: for interactive flows we need p95 < 300ms for short prompts at 100 qps sustained, and for long generations we need p95 < 1.2s when generating ~800 tokens with streaming enabled. Cost target is under $0.08 per 1k tokens across our production mix. If we can't hit both latency and cost, we need to understand tradeoffs.

[01:52] Daniel Park: That's helpful. We should be explicit: p95 300ms for short prompts is tight but achievable on dedicated GPU pools with batching off for those short requests; streaming adds additional overhead but can reduce perceived latency because of first-byte earlier. For long generations, streaming actually helps perceived latency but sometimes increases total CPU/GPU inefficiency if the model can't batch large tails.

[02:15] Alex Chen: Can you talk through what exactly you want for the harness? We currently use Locust for HTTP-level tests and a small Python async client for streaming in our staging.

[02:26] Daniel Park: Our recommended approach is a hybrid: k6 for non-streaming bulk runs (easy to ramp and collect p95/p99) and a lightweight asyncio-based runner for streaming tests that consumes SSE/Chunked responses and measures first-byte and token delta times. We'll share both. The harness will include: user/session patterns, backoff, ramping steps, and payload generators that mimic your token length distribution.

[02:49] Priya Rao: For streaming measurement, what's the granularity? We want to capture first-byte, token emission times, and overall time-to-end.

[02:58] Daniel Park: We'll instrument the client to emit timestamps for first_byte, token_50 (when 50% tokens emitted), token_90, and final_end. That gives you a clear view of how streaming changes perceived latency. Also capture server-side metrics (if you can share CloudWatch/Prometheus spans) like GPU utilization, queue length, and batching windows.

[03:20] Alex Chen: Regarding load shape, our peak is around 350 concurrent users, translating to roughly 220 qps for short requests during spikes, and about 30 concurrent long runs (these last 40-90s each). We can produce a histogram of token lengths.

[03:37] Maya Collins: Perfect. For modeling this in the harness we will create two scenarios: steady short-prompt steady-state and mixed-scenario where short and long requests interleave according to your histogram. We'll run non-streaming baseline first, then run streaming with identical input to measure delta.

[03:54] Michael Thompson: One question: does streaming change batching? I worry that if we enable streaming we lose some batching benefits and that could blow our cost.

[04:05] Daniel Park: Short answer: yes, streaming can reduce batching efficiency because tokens are flushed to the network earlier. But Redwood's serving runtime supports small-window continuous batching and prefix caching—so for many workloads we still get decent utilization. We'll show you kernel selection and quantization profiles that help. Also we can recommend different rollout policies: use streaming for interactive routes and non-streaming for background generation.

[04:34] Alex Chen: When you say prefix caching, will it help repeated prompts? We have common starter prompts reused across sessions.

[04:40] Daniel Park: Exactly. Prefix/KV cache will reduce token compute for repeats and reduce latency for repeated prefixes. For benchmark fairness we should include a cold cache baseline and a warmed cache run to show delta.

[04:55] Priya Rao: Network is another constraint — our SRE team wants to understand egress and latency to Redwood's region. We might run the harness from our VPC via a private peering connection. Is that supported for the POC?

[05:07] Maya Collins: Yes, we support private peering for POC runs; we'll coordinate a narrow maintenance window with your infra to open the necessary egress and peering. We'll give a small set of IPs and short-lived credentials.

[05:18] Alex Chen: Ok. For the scripts, we need examples for both k6 vscript and a Python async client that handles chunked transfer encoding and reconnection/backoff.

[05:29] Sofia Ruiz: We'll include a sample 'stream_consumer.py' that connects, logs timestamps for first_byte and token emissions, and shows how to parse SSE vs chunked JSON. Also a 'k6_short_p0.js' that hits the non-streaming endpoint with ramp stages. The sample harness will include instructions to run locally and in CI.

[05:50] Michael Thompson: Can we also benchmark embeddings? We use embeddings for search and need to know p95 for batch-embedding of 256 vectors and cost per 1k vectors.

[05:59] Daniel Park: Sure — embeddings are straightforward: we'll run batch sizes of 1, 16, 64, 256 and capture throughput and GPU occupancy. We'll include those scenarios in the spreadsheet.

[06:12] Alex Chen: A pragmatic timeline would be: we share traces by Thursday, you provide harness by Sunday, Quantara runs an initial non-streaming baseline the following week, then we run streaming experiments after that. Are those dates realistic?

[06:24] Maya Collins: Realistic; we can commit to the harness by 2025-04-13 and a proposed baseline run window 2025-04-24. We'll also share an example report template so results are comparable.

[06:36] Priya Rao: About measurement — we want to see p50, p95, p99, error rates, retries, average tokens generated, and cost. Will you include token counts in the logs?

[06:47] Daniel Park: Yes, every response will log request_token_count and response_token_count, plus total_cost_estimate using your pricing profile. For streaming we will also compute cost-per-response and incremental cost-per-token.

[06:58] Alex Chen: Great. I want to call out a constraint: during the POC we can't expose raw content off our VPC. So we need options: 1) run harness from our side and ship metrics back to Redwood, or 2) allow Redwood to run in a customer-managed sandbox with logs kept in your account. Which is easier?

[07:12] Maya Collins: Both are options. Many customers prefer to run the harness in their VPC and share summary metrics (CSV/JSON). If you want Redwood to run it, we can arrange a private sandbox that writes logs to your S3 bucket and never retains content in our control plane. We'll document both options in the runbook.

[07:30] Michael Thompson: For the benchmarking runs, do you have recommendations on ramp profile? We want to avoid sudden spikes that will trip autoscaling in a way that does not reflect real behavior.

[07:42] Daniel Park: We usually do a 15-minute ramp: 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 75% -> 100% over 15 minutes, hold for 30-60 minutes, then step down. We'll also run a spike test where we inject a 30s 2x burst to evaluate graceful degradation and fallback policies. We'll capture model fallback, latency increases, and error surfaces.

[08:02] Priya Rao: Are you able to simulate synthetic user think-times? We have user sessions with intermittent typing and idle times.

[08:10] Sofia Ruiz: Yes, the harness includes session patterns with think-time distributions (exponential backoff, power-law sessions). We'll give you a scenario file where you can tweak mean think time and concurrency.

[08:22] Alex Chen: What about instrumentation? If we run in our VPC and only share metrics, how granular will the report be?

[08:30] Daniel Park: We'll standardize the output: per-request timestamps, latency percentiles, token counts, error codes, and aggregated GPU metrics every 30s. The report will include CSVs and a human-readable PDF with charts.

[08:41] Michael Thompson: One more ops question — can we pin a model version and quantization profile for the baseline? We want to ensure reproducibility across runs.

[08:50] Maya Collins: Absolutely. We'll propose a stable model revision and quantization profile for the POC. We'll also record the runtime kernel selection and compile flags so results are auditable.

[09:00] Alex Chen: Let's talk numbers for the baseline: start non-streaming with 200 qps short prompt run for 30 minutes (target p95 < 300ms). Then run mixed-scenario at 220 qps peak with long runs included, measure p95 for long of <1.2s. Then streaming run with same mixture to compare first_byte metrics.

[09:18] Daniel Park: That plan makes sense. For long-run p95 we may need to tolerate slightly higher p95 if token counts are super high; we'll include per-token-slabed percentiles. Also we'll run a cold-cache vs warm-cache comparison to be transparent about cache impact.

[09:34] Priya Rao: For cost modeling, please include a simple spreadsheet that computes cost = compute_cost + infra_markup + network, with an estimate per 100k requests and per 1M tokens. That helps procurement.

[09:45] Maya Collins: We'll attach a template. Also we'll include sensitivity knobs: batching target, quant profile, and autoscaling buffer.

[09:56] Alex Chen: Any gotchas we should know about before running?

[10:01] Daniel Park: A few: 1) if you stream heavily you'll see different tail behaviors depending on the client's TCP Nagle/flush settings, so use the provided stream_consumer.py that flushes promptly; 2) identical prompt text can trigger different kernels if tokenization differs, so keep tokenizers consistent; 3) ensure you warm or clear caches intentionally when comparing cold/warm runs.

[10:21] Sofia Ruiz: We'll also include a small checklist for SRE: open ports, IPs, TLS certs, and minimum instance sizes if you decide to host the harness in a sandbox.

[10:33] Michael Thompson: Ok sounds good. Who will own the first-run coordination? Quantara will run harness in our staging and send results to Redwood?

[10:41] Maya Collins: Either works. Based on the notes, we'll send the harness and instructions; if you choose to run it in your VPC, send the metrics CSV and we'll analyze. If you'd like Redwood to run it, we'll need the peering window and sandbox creds.

[10:55] Alex Chen: We'll start by running it ourselves. Priya will coordinate with infra for peering windows if needed.

[11:03] Maya Collins: Great. Quick recap of concrete next steps: Redwood share harness and report template by 2025-04-13; Quantara share anonymized traces by 2025-04-17; Quantara runs non-streaming baseline 2025-04-24, then streaming tests and embeds follow. We'll reconvene 2025-04-28 to review.

[11:20] Priya Rao: Sounds good. One last Q: what logs do you keep if Redwood runs the test? We want assurance that content isn't retained.

[11:28] Daniel Park: We'll propose an S3-only export with lifecycle rules and an explicit retention agreement for the POC. We'll never ingest trace content into our long-term control plane for the POC unless you opt in. We'll include that language in the runbook.

[11:41] Maya Collins: Thanks everyone. We'll send the zip and runbook. Any final comments?

[11:47] Michael Thompson: No, thanks. Appreciate the level of detail.

[11:50] Alex Chen: Thanks. We'll follow-up on the traces.

[11:52] End of recording.

Notes about transcript: Some words may be mis-transcribed (e.g., kernel names, internal product names) and timestamps are approximations every ~15-40s. There is occasional overlap and filler words preserved to maintain authenticity.
